[38;5;231m●[39m [1mThe Last Keeper[0m

  For forty-one years, Marguerite Olsen climbed the one hundred and twelve steps of the Breakwater Point lighthouse
  every evening at dusk. She knew each step by its sound: the seventh creaked, the thirtieth rang hollow, and the
  ninety-fourth had a chip on its edge she'd learned to step past without looking.

  The Coast Guard had automated the light in 1989. A man in a pressed uniform came out with a clipboard and a box of
  electronics and told her, kindly, that she was no longer needed. The lamp would turn itself on. The fog signal would
  sound by itself. She could stay in the keeper's cottage, he said, as long as she liked.

  So she stayed, and she kept climbing.

  The sensor turned the lamp on at dusk, but it didn't wipe the salt off the lens, so Marguerite did. It didn't notice
  when gulls nested in the gallery railing, or when rust started creeping under the paint on the north window. It didn't
  know that the Pelletier boy took his father's skiff out past the shoals on nights he shouldn't, or that old Ambrose
  Tull, who'd been half-blind since the war, still fished by the light's rhythm, counting four seconds dark and one
  second bright.

  On the night of the November storm, the power went out across the whole peninsula. The backup generator coughed twice
  and died. Marguerite was already halfway up the stairs when the light went black.

  She'd kept the old kerosene lamp. Nobody had asked her to, and nobody had told her not to. She carried it up the last
  steps, her knees aching, the wind screaming through the gaps in the glass. She lit it with shaking hands and set it in
  the old cradle behind the lens, and the great prism took the small flame and threw it miles out over the water.

  She turned the lens by hand all night: four seconds dark, one second bright.

  At dawn, the Pelletier boy's skiff limped into the harbor with a cracked hull and the boy shivering at the tiller. He
  told everyone he'd been lost in the black until he saw the light, faint but steady, and followed it home.

  The Coast Guard sent a new generator the next week. The man with the clipboard came too, and this time he took off his
  hat when he knocked on her door.
